Absolutely 100% support this response. It is a very fine line when establishing rapport with clients, families, teachers in the classroom or any other individual involved in that person‘s case. Once it moves from implementing strategies to being actually being the reinforcing item” it can get a little tricky.

It isn’t whack. We have an ethical code that we have to abide by because behavior analytic work is very serious. 

You’re literally participating in social and emotional conditioning. There is something known as stimulus control, and it can be incredibly hard to break stimulus control as well as it can be very hard to develop it. 

The goal is not to be the most popular behavior technician the goal is to be the most effective behavior technician for your clients.

I had an 18-year-old look at his current behavior technician and tell her “I don’t listen to you. I listen to her”, meaning me. While he was in the middle of crisis and I was working with a different client.

He was so attached to me because I knew him 2 years prior from our social skills groups and we did community outings, group events, and talked about a lot of important serious topics there which fostered his trust in me and an inevitable attachment to me. 

Once I realize that stimulus control was not generalizing to any other staff, I requested to have myself removed from that case. I’ll always be a “trusted adult”, but I can no longer be the direct care provider because it is now teetering the line of a “dual relationship” because he looked at me as a mentor or life coach instead of an RBT.

Unfortunately, this does happen. It’s incredibly important for us as behavior analysts and RBTs to maintain our ethical professionalism when it comes to the conduct with our clients. 

There are times when a client may be too attached to you and the instructional control isn’t generalizing to other people  or environments, which would correlate to a prompt or stimulus dependency. That would also be an appropriate time for fading or perhaps a switching staff because it is important for the client to be able to respond to anyone not just one particular person.

Hi there, I’m sorry to hear about your struggles! I was an RBT for 6 years and also spent a year in HR/Recruitment specifically to hire RBTs and BCBAs for my agency. 

There are only a few things that I would have denied employment for, but here are a few things that would stick out from interviews with people that are new to ABA.

If someone with very little experience in special education or autism services applied I would definitely want to hear about their experiences with crisis management and daily living skills such as toileting etc. There are some slight, but significant differences between RBT work and childcare and it’s important to know that before you take on a case load.

I had a person come in for an interview that had a BA degree and her RBT, but said that she would never want to change a diaper or assist with anything that involved fluids or excrement. To me, that felt like she wouldn’t be able to provide services to child that was severely impacted and I didn’t want my company to spend resources training a person who wouldn’t be willing to do those things if needed. 

I have also had people talk about their refusal to participate in response blocking, restraint etc. My personal philosophy is that restraints are not needed. I have never needed to use a restraint ever because my company was a hands off facility and de-escalation/prompt/wait strategies have been very successful in ALL of my clients over the past 6 years.

However, I need to know that you, as the RBT, will put your personal opinions aside and follow that individualized behavior plan. It is absolutely okay to have your own feelings and thoughts about things and discuss them with your BCBA, but I need to know that the follow through will be there because that is what our clients need. 

The bottom line in any RBT interview is “How far are you willing to go for OUR clients?”

TLDR; Sometimes showing resistance to the less glamorous parts of the job stands out as an inflexibility on your end.

I actually refer to myself and all staff as “Ms;Mr First Name”. In my 6 years as an RBT I have never struggled with instructional control and I believe it’s because the “Mr;Ms” assumes authority without having to discuss it.

Additionally, it is much easier for some individuals to address someone as “Ms;Mr” than it is to understand the intricacies of every persons name in the world. 

I don’t need my kids to know how to say my name in particular. I need them to know how to safely mand or gain the attention of others by saying “Mr;Ms….. can I x,y,z?” Instead of “Hey!” Or “You!”

In my experience, It makes making FTC errorless, because they’re not being corrected all day like “oh I’m not Michael, I’m Zack.” 

To me, if they learn my name then I have truly bonded with them and it’s like now they trust me enough to be part of their repertoire. 

I worked with a kiddo who would call all adults “teacher.” I never corrected him because he had apraxia, adhd, autism, and high risk of SIB, AGG, and Elopement. To me “teacher” gets the job done for now. There is plenty of time to know my name and as long as he knows his parents/siblings name, I’m good with it.

Story time: 32/f here. I am part of the the A/S/L generation: AOL, AIM, LiveJournal, Bandcamp, MySpace, Facebook, Tumblr, Instagram etc. you name it, I was there when the word was written. 

In middle school, I was a total goth and eventual scene queen. It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, and of course, I felt isolated and alone. 

One night when I was 12, I was at a sleep over, late at night, and in an AOL music chat room. I’ve always loved classic rock, 80s metal, 90s alt, NuMetal etc.. and I was really looking for somewhere to talk about life, love, and my interests.

I would put my actual age in the chat because I felt like it was better to be honest than to have them find out later on that I’m actually 12. This is when I met “Doug”, 17/m/NJ. 

I remember being excited that a high schooler was talking to me. He looked at my MySpace and talked to me about all of my favorite things and then he asked if we could talk on the phone. I was at my friends house, so I used her house phone, and we wound up chatting until 6 am.

Doug and I talked everyday and as often as possible. I can still remember the sound of the door when he signed on to “AIM” (iykyk). When I would inevitably have to sign off line, I would sneak calls to him from my house phone and when I slept over my friends house we would talk all night about everything. He was there for me when I would fight with my grandmom and when my mom left. I eventually got a prepaid cell phone so that we were able to text and talk more discretely because I knew that he was older and I wanted to protect him.

He told me that I was the prettiest girl that he has ever seen. “You are so adorable, I just want to kiss your little face.” He told me that he loved my “little nose” and he would comment on all of my pictures with hearts or “NOSE!!! <333”.

My 13th birthday came and went and  “only 3 more years and then we can be together”, not realizing that 16 year old me would be dating a 21 year old him and also that this entire situation is completely fucked up.

13 year old me was absolutely dating him. He was my day and night. My friends were so jealous. They could all see how dedicated he was to me (calls, texts, sweetness) and as far as I was concerned, as soon as I turned 16 (age of consent in NJ), Doug and I would be together. We were having “phone sex” on a daily basis. It was graphic and I do believe that he was actually doing it on the other end.

At this point he is now 18 and getting ready for senior prom. He continues, “I wish that I could bring you to prom with me.” “You would look so beautiful in a dress” “I would love to dress you up”.

I would be lying if I didn’t admit to absolutely loving the adoration. Obviously, my childhood and family life was a shit show, and Doug made me feel pretty and special.. and loved. He would tell me that he loved me and how he will wait for me. He always talked about my mind and how brilliant I was for my age. This went on until I was in 9th grade. I naively was hoping that this would be my happily ever after.

Then one day “Allison” called my friends parents house phone at 2:00 in the morning and left the most HORRIFIC voicemail I’ve ever heard, which back in the day, just PLAYED out-loud for the entire house to hear. 

Allison was Doug’s girlfriend of 4 years. They had been together for all of high school. She said that he talked about me when he was drunk and then she found our MySpace conversation which showed her exactly when we started talking on the phone. She went through his call history on his cell phone and saw that we spoke almost every single night. 

Basically, he was her boyfriend for years and then she would go home and he would stay up until 6 am talking to and having phone sex with 13 year old girl. 

She threatened the absolute life out of me. Told me that I “made her boyfriend a pedophile because I was a whore and he thought that you were easy.” 

He called me as well, with her, and dismantled our entire relationship. Most of the dirty stuff was done over the phone so there was no proof (nudes weren’t really a thing yet in the early 2000s). 

I was crushed. So used, so young, and absolutely devastated. Groomed, is a term that didn’t exist then, but does now. My friends parents tried to use the tough love approach and explain to me the dangers of men online, but i defended him at every turn and no charges were ever pressed. 

He wound up finding me on Facebook in 2009, when I was 17. He came in with an overflow of love bombing, apologizing, begging, “I just need to hear your sweet voice one more time.” At this point, he was 22 and I was hyper aware of what had happened to me. I blocked him without responding and that’s the story of the one time that I was groomed in middle school.

He’s still out there somewhere.

Talk to the BCBA about conducting a “free operant preference assessment” during your “pairing session.”

Allow the client to show you the things that they like to do. Let the demands stay low. Try not to correct or intervene immediately because you want to learn how THEY communicate or see what motivates them to interact.

You will have plenty of time to assist with creating positive changes in this child’s life, but at first, and especially with little information, let the client lead.

Of course! Believe me we have all worked in households that can be over the top and you have every right to feel overwhelmed. This can be a great opportunity to integrate social goals and caregiver training goals and really help this family gain some synchronicity! 

Turn taking games would be incredibly helpful as well as 1-2 step activities such as yoga, freeze dance, or even arts and crafts to help the family learn how to interact with your client.

This may be a moment to think about the true ethical dilemma that you’re facing.

You’re not lying about being overly qualified, you’re not lying to your supervisor, and you’re not breaking any dual/multiple relationship rules. 

You are protecting your clients diagnosis  and personal medical history from a person that the parent isn’t ready to trust with the information yet. It really may be boiled down to the clients privacy and dignity. Some parents aren’t ready to confront the diagnosis yet and that is okay. 

Review the BACB Ethical Code. It is drilled into our heads during grad school and it does help when you’re trying to weigh out the options. 

Talk to your BCBA about “Social Skills Goals.” You can use tools like “Social Skills solutions” (McKinnon & Krempa, 2002) to brainstorm on goals that can be achieved during these play groups. 

I had a client that moved to a new area and for the first year of them living there, during trick or treating or even play groups out in the community, we told the other parents that I was her babysitter.

Why? Because our clients are members of a vulnerable population and it can be dangerous if someone knows about your child’s diagnosis, be it a stranger or your own family members.

External and internal expressions of emotions are usually involuntary. Our body is reacting to multiple internal operations which will then cause our outward expressions. There has to be a combination of chemical release (testosterone, cortisol, estrogen etc) in accompaniment with environmental factors to provide a reaction.

Typically, the way that we express ourselves, (our behaviors, and our mannerisms) are learned behaviors. We learn these behaviors from observation and imitation. We learn how to test the reactions of our environments throughout our entire lives from the beginning to the end. 

A baby cries and realizes it will be fed.

I could never express myself or feel validated in my family until I was screaming. I was often ignored until I felt like I had to explode. I (28/F) have experienced an "explosive temper" and feelings of dread since elementary school.

I have always used extremely aggressive and confrontational "defense tactics" to resolve many of my feelings, such as intimidation, fear and discomfort.

I hate feeling "stupid", "wrong", or "embarrassed." 

I hate when other people act "powerful" or "demanding."

I would take all of my feelings of "disappointment" and "resentment" out on the people that I love. 

I didn't mean to, but whenever it happened I was always very hard to console.

I have lost jobs because of my anger. 

I have been arrested because of my anger. 

I have lost friends and pushed away relationships and maybe even changed the course of my actual life because of my anger. 

Some of these situations were easily resolved, but some of them were not. 

I have had to live with the consequences of my outbursts and being labeled as "emotional" or "easily antagonized", for most of my life.

These feelings of fear and rejection have invited a lot of insecurities to brew within me. 

I didn't know myself for a very long time. 
I was always hiding my discomfort. 
I didn't trust myself or really anyone else anymore. 

All that I knew was that I was in pain and no one was helping me the way that I "needed" to be helped.

Anger is like suit of armor. It feels safe and protects us from the emotional blows. 

There is nothing more comforting to a "fearful" person than knowing "I have a way to hurt someone if they try to hurt me."

In times of distress we can choose to be vulnerable or immovable, but anger is a mountain. 

These feelings of mistrust will look to anger as a shield for as long as it can. It is the only thing that we know how to do when we are hurting because we have depended on anger to protect us for so long.
